_comment: Words whose two meanings change what an adult should do. When one of these appears in a child's text, the app always asks the child which they meant; it never guesses. Asking the model alone proved unreliable: it knows these ambiguities when asked directly, but reports them inconsistently inside a judging task, and a knife threat that loses its timing is not something to leave to chance. The model check still runs alongside this and catches what the list does not. Each entry must be reviewed by a team member who speaks the language; this is a vocabulary question, so getting it wrong is visible. 25 Oct: 'maarna' removed after review. A child writing it is alive, so offering them 'kills' as a reading is impossible to answer and frightening; the hit/kill risk is a translation error for the judge, not a question for the child. 'kal' now carries skip_when so tense settles it where it can. 26 Oct: every language's list is read whatever language the child's screens are in, because a child on English screens may still write Hindi ('kal chhutti ke baad'). Another language's words match as whole words only, and its skip_when is not applied, since in mixed text those grammar markers collide with the screen language (Hindi 'the' is English 'the'). See lexicon_ambiguities in engine/translate.py. An entry may set "ask_first": true when it decides WHETHER something is a threat; only two questions ever reach the child, so those are asked before words that only decide when or who.

hi.note: Hindi uses one word for both. With a threat this is the difference between something about to happen and something already over. Only asked when the sentence carries no tense marker: with one, the tense decides, and asking anyway spends a question the child does not owe us. Since a list match also forces the full check, asking about every 'kal' cost latency as well.

skip_when._comment: Tense decides 'kal' nearly always: a future verb makes it tomorrow, a past one yesterday. Only ask when neither is present. The Devanagari patterns use lookarounds, not \b: a vowel sign such as ा (U+093E) is not a word character in Python's re, so \b never matches after one and those patterns silently never fired. The Devanagari future pattern needs the vowel a future ending carries before ग (मारेगा, आएगा, आएंगे, करूँगा, करोगे): ending in -गा/-गी/-गे alone also matches nouns such as ज़िंदगी (life) and मुर्गी (hen), and a skip that fires on a noun makes the app silently choose between yesterday and tomorrow. The listed words have that vowel and are still not verbs, so they never count; गूंगा (mute) is listed because a child may be called it.

hi.note: Caught in the Hindi benchmark: 'kal chhutti ke baad chaaku leke aayega' was translated as 'after the holidays', so a knife threat for tomorrow lost its timing.
